title: Example 18-6: Text with Limited Insertions and Corrections

illustrates.quote:
When a text shows limited insertions and corrections within the flow of text:
a. Use a transcriber-defined typeform indicator to show the crossed-out word(s). (See UEB, §9.5, Transcriber-Defined Typeform Indicators.)
b. Explain the usage in a transcriber’s note.

blocks.text: Transcriber's note: "The symbol [transcriber-defined strike-through mark] indicates a crossed-out word." (back-translated, matches both runs); the sentence itself, "Sarah *like* likes vanilla ice cream." with "like" struck through and marked by the transcriber-defined mark ^#1 — not modeled: F-188 (only one hardcoded transcriber-defined symbol exists at all, already used elsewhere for the print asterism, so a second one for strike-through cannot be minted).

print.notes: The word "like" has a horizontal strikethrough in print.

braille.notes: Re-extracted from source (lines 14552-14555, margin 9); matches both runs byte-for-byte.

resolution: Braille already agreed and re-extraction confirms it exactly. print.blocks kept as a single 'other' (F-188) rather than attempting a plain-text sentence: unlike example-18-2’s list (where the missing mark is a simple prefix before otherwise-independent names), here the mark (^#1) is the ENTIRE point of the example (marking a specific crossed-out word inline) and the sentence without it reads as ordinary, unmarked prose that would not exercise what this example demonstrates at all.
